---
title: "Difference Arrays: Mark Where Changes Begin and End"
description: "A mathematical technique worth memorising for algorithm interviews."
---

## Recognition trigger

Many interval increments, imos technique, range additions and sweep-line events.

## Problem to think through

**Why update every element of an interval when just two boundaries change?**

## Formula worth memorising

$$
D[l]\mathrel{+}=v,\qquad D[r+1]\mathrel{-}=v
$$

**Every symbol explained:** D is a difference array; [l,r] is the inclusive interval; v is the increment applied to each element; += and −= change the two boundary markers. Reconstruct A by taking the prefix sum of D.

**Substitute actual values:** Start A=[0,0,0,0,0]. To add 3 to indices [1,3], mark D[1]+=3 and D[4]−=3. Prefix-summing those markers yields [0,3,3,3,0].

## Why the derivation is valid

The +v event begins the extra contribution at l; the −v event cancels it immediately after r. Between the boundaries, every prefix includes +v but not −v, so exactly the desired interval receives the update.

## What could invalidate it?

This is effective when you can process all updates before asking for final point values. Online range queries/updates may require a Fenwick or segment tree instead.

## The 20-second memory card

**Memorise: Range update = start event plus reverse event after the interval; one prefix pass reconstructs all values.**

Reconstruct the proof from the example rather than memorising the code.

**Interview problems:** Corporate Flight Bookings; Range Addition.

**Research reference:** [Read the mathematical method](https://usaco.guide/silver/prefix-sums). The worked numbers and explanation are independently written.
